sections.heading: Finding my comfort in you alone
sections.text: Father, your will rules over everything, and I do not want to look for comfort where you are not. Nothing can truly satisfy me apart from knowing you, enjoying you, and serving you. Every good thing in my life is only as good as you make it. Without you, even my happiest moments are empty; with you, ordinary gifts become signs of your kindness.
theological_themes: God is the source and measure of all true joy, comfort, and service; created pleasures are good only as received from him and enjoyed in relation to him.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God himself is his deepest desire and lasting portion, even when every created strength fails. This grounds the prayer’s claim that comfort is found ultimately in God, not in the gifts apart from him.
James teaches that every good gift comes from God. That supports the prayer’s insistence that all enjoyments are dependent on God’s giving and goodness.

sections.heading: Trusting your will more than my own judgment
sections.text: I want to be glad in whatever you choose, even when I do not understand it yet. If you gave me the choice in any matter, I would rather place the whole thing back into your hands. You are perfectly wise, and you never make a wrong move. I do. So teach me to rest in the fact that everything belongs to your care. It is a relief to leave my life, my plans, and my unanswered questions with you.
theological_themes: God’s sovereign wisdom is safer than human self-direction; surrender is not passivity but trust in God’s perfect rule.

scripture_references.connection: This passage calls God’s people not to lean on their own understanding but to trust him in all their ways. It directly supports the movement from self-decision to entrusting decisions to God’s wisdom.
Paul speaks of God working all things according to the counsel of his will. That gives biblical weight to the prayer’s comfort in knowing that all things are at God’s disposal.

sections.heading: Letting prayer become praise
sections.text: When I remember that you hold all things wisely and well, my asking turns into worship. I do not know what I could possibly give back to you for all your kindness. I want to respond, but I have nothing that did not first come from you. So I bless you because the glory is yours alone. No one in heaven or on earth can share the honor that belongs to you.
theological_themes: Gratitude leads to adoration; because God is the giver of all things, human response cannot repay him but can praise him.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks what he can render to the Lord for all his benefits and answers with worshipful, covenantal response. This closely reflects the prayer’s movement from receiving God’s mercy to asking how to respond.
Paul concludes that all things are from, through, and to God, and therefore glory belongs to him forever. This supports the prayer’s insistence that God alone receives the honor.

sections.heading: Offering myself because grace makes even that possible
sections.text: By myself, I cannot add anything to your glory or make your name greater. But by your grace, I can give myself to you gladly. Take my whole life—my soul, my body, my desires, my work, my future. I belong to you, and I want to live that way.
theological_themes: The believer’s self-offering is a grace-enabled response to God, not a contribution that earns merit or completes God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers, in view of God’s mercies, to present their bodies as living sacrifices. This supports the prayer’s desire to surrender soul and body as a grateful response to grace.
Paul challenges boasting by asking what anyone has that they did not receive. This illumines the prayer’s confession that even what is offered back to God first comes from him.

sections.heading: Confessing that salvation and every good desire come from you
sections.text: Lord Jesus, you began my faith, and you will bring it to completion. The whole rescue of my life is your work from start to finish. Any good thought, any honest prayer, any step of obedience, any desire to please you—none of it starts with me. It is the effect of your power and grace. You work in me to want what is good and to do what pleases you, simply because this is your good pleasure.
theological_themes: Faith, redemption, obedience, and holy desire are gifts of divine grace; God initiates and completes the saving work.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews identifies Jesus as the founder and perfecter of faith. This directly grounds the confession that faith begins and is completed by Christ rather than by human strength.

Paul calls believers to active obedience while grounding that obedience in God’s work within them to will and to work for his good pleasure. This matches the prayer’s dependence on God for both desire and action.

Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, and that good works are prepared by God. This supports both the denial of human boasting and the affirmation that obedience flows from grace.

sections.heading: Being honest about what I am without your mercy
sections.text: God, it shocks me how easily people speak as though we are naturally strong and good on our own. I know enough of my own heart to say otherwise. If you did not hold me back and keep me moment by moment, I would run toward evil with terrifying speed. You have taught me this about myself—not as a theory, but through painful experience. Keep me humble, keep me dependent, and keep me close to you.
theological_themes: Human nature is deeply corrupted by sin; any restraint from evil and any perseverance in good are due to God’s preserving mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Paul gathers Old Testament testimony to describe the pervasive corruption of human sin apart from grace. This supports the prayer’s severe honesty about what people are apart from God’s restraining and saving work.
Paul confesses that nothing good dwells in his flesh, even while he desires what is right. This illumines the prayer’s personal, experiential self-knowledge about the danger within the human heart.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God to preserve and restrain the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly reflects Reformed/Puritan emphases on divine sovereignty, human inability, and total dependence on grace. These are biblical themes, but the way they are formulated can be doctrinally contested among Christian traditions.

The line implying that without God’s continual restraint humans would be “devils incarnate” is deliberately severe. I preserved its force as a confession of radical moral danger apart from grace, while avoiding language that would imply humans literally cease to be human or become demons.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “all enjoyments are what to me thou makest them” as meaning that created pleasures have true value only as God gives, governs, and blesses them, not as a rejection of created goods themselves.

I interpreted “if thou bidst me decide for myself” as a prayer of yielded decision-making rather than an avoidance of responsibility; the modern wording keeps the desire to entrust judgment to God while still allowing for ordinary obedience and action.
I rendered the desire to “make some return” as gratitude that cannot repay God. This preserves the original tension: the believer longs to respond but has nothing independent to offer.
I treated “author and finisher of faith” as explicitly Christological in line with Hebrews 12:2, while keeping the wider address to God consistent with the prayer’s Trinitarian section context.
